extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying transfer and licensing of patent rights
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and doctrines governing assignment, sale, and implied licenses of patented articles — including territorial limits, conditions, and consequences of sales by patentees, licensees, and judicial officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: License assignability (gross sum)
rubrics_metrics.description: That a license to use an invention to a certain extent on payment of a gross sum is prima facie assignable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: "That a license to use the invention to a certain extent on payment of a gross sum is prima facie assignable," with cases cited (e.g., Belding v. Turner). Shows that licenses payable by lump sum are generally assignable absent contrary terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: License to partnership is valid when prepaid
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to a partnership is good, if paid for in advance, though one member of the firm retires and new members are admitted, unless the contrary is expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example citations: Belding v. Turner (1871). Explains that interest of partners in a prepaid license survives changes in firm composition unless license states otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive license vests in personal representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an exclusive right is granted to a licensee it vests at his death in his personal representatives so far as to enable them to finish up and dispose of the devices on hand, and then ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Pitts v. Jameson (1853). Practical consequence: executors can complete existing business but cannot extend the license beyond winding up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized transfer may be ratified by acceptance of royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: An unauthorized transfer of a license may be ratified by the acceptance of the royalties or license-fees from the assignee after notice of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensor accepts payments from assignee after learning of assignment, licensor may be taken to have validated the transfer (see Wilde v. Smith and Bloomer v. Gilpin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignees take subject to original license obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignees of a license take it subject to all the obligations and conditions imposed upon the original licensee, and run their own risk of his right to transfer it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized transfers do not free assignees from contractual limitations; purchaser bears risk of vendor's authority to sell (see Chambers v. Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license from lawful, unconditional sale of patented article
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawful and unconditional sale of a patented article by one with a right to sell carries an implied license to the purchaser, and to every subsequent owner of the article, to use it as long as its identity can be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal rule (Adams v. Burke and others): sale emancipates the article from the monopoly; purchaser may use and resell it without further liability so long as sale was lawful and unconditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale must be lawful and unconditional to free article from monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: To have the emancipating effect, the sale must be lawful and an unconditional sale; the sale is lawful when the vendor is the patentee or one to whom he has conveyed the right to sell without conditions, or one on whom such right has been conferred by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sale is conditional or by someone without authority to sell, the implied license may not arise. Cases: Porter Needle Co. v. National Needle Co., McKeever v. United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may sever ownership from right to use
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may sever the ownership of a patented article from the right to use it; a machine may be sold without the right to use it, and purchaser then does not acquire a right to use by the sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Rodgers v. Torrant, Wortendyke v. White, Wilson v. Stolley. Patentee can sell physical object but retain monopoly rights to restrict use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license requires sale of the identical patented article
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale from which the universal license is implied must be a sale of the precise article covered by the patent; purchasers of mere materials or parts do not thereby obtain right to make and use the patented article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: where an object can be used only in constructing a patented article, sale of that object by patentee implies license to use it for that purpose (see Roosevelt v. Western Electric). If article is broken up, purchaser of parts cannot reconstruct and claim right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of combination or manufactured article by patentee conveys right to use combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of the complete article by one who owns a patent for the materials or the combination carries a license to employ the materials in the article, or the elements in combination, and to use them thus united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where seller is patentee and sells the assembled product, the buyer may use it even if the patentee also has patents on components; cited: Goodyear v. Beverly Rubber Co., and other authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license includes right to repair and to sell; duration unlimited
rubrics_metrics.description: The implied license of the purchaser and his vendees includes the right to use, the right to repair, and the right to sell; the right to use is unlimited in duration and continues through patent term and extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section §826: Unlike some express licenses, the implied license survives patent extensions, including special acts of Congress that extend patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconditional market sale produces unrestricted use rights
rubrics_metrics.description: When the sale is unconditional, as in ordinary sales by authorized vendors in open market, the implied license gives purchaser and his vendees the unrestricted right to use and resell the article unless such use infringes some other patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: unrestricted sale does not permit infringement of different patents covering methods or replacement parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sellers may impose conditions limiting use (time/place/method/quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A seller may at the time of sale restrict the use of his vendee within specific boundaries of time, place, method, or quantity, and these conditions become the measure of the implied license arising from the sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Holliday v. Matheson; parties may contract territorial or temporal restraints and those bind purchasers and vendees if properly expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial assignments transfer limited rights (territorial v. personal right distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of rights "within a given territory" transfers a territorial right (right to make, use, sell within that territory and to license others there) but does not transfer the patentee's personal right to confer rights everywhere; grantee cannot license outside the assigned territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed exposition: the patentee's personal right is the whole monopoly; territorial grantees have rights limited to area; if patentee intended broader power, must be expressly stated in assignment (see Billings cases and critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser takes risk of vendor's authority to sell
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser of a licensee's right must take his own risks as to the vendor's right to sell; if vendor lacked authority, purchaser may suffer consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chambers v. Smith and related authorities: buyer cannot necessarily rely on apparent title — runs risk of vendor's defective power to transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of royalties from assignee after notice evidences ratification
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance by the licensor of royalties or demand for payment from the assignee after notice of assignment shows the licensor knew of the assignment and may validate an assignment contrary to the license terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Wilde v. Smith; notice plus acceptance may estop licensor from asserting transfer invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses bind assignees whether recorded or not
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses bind, as to terms and obligations, all assignees of the licensee, whether the license is recorded or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: third parties acquiring under licensee are subject to the same covenants; cases: Hamilton v. Kingsbury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of license on royalty resembles lease assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a license granted for an annual royalty resembles the assignment of a lease and follows the same rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant case: Wilde v. Smith; treat license with recurring royalties analogously to tenancy assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale by licensee under authority releases machines from monopoly like patentee's sale
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale by a licensee acting within the authority conferred by an assignment or license releases the machine from the monopoly in the same way as a sale by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensee validly sells machines under his license, purchasers acquire the same implied rights as if bought from patentee (Howe v. Wooldredge; Birdsell v. Sharlow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale abroad without restriction can free article in US if seller had right to sell
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale of a patented article abroad by an assignee or licensee without restrictions may free the article from the monopoly and permit purchaser to use and sell it in the United States, subject to territorial scope of grants and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Holliday v. Matheson and McKay v. Wooster — but caution: territorial assignments and seller intent may limit effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of articles containing components under other patents carries limited license
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of a machine which contains elements (e.g., needles) covered by a different patent of the same patentee carries a license to use those elements until they are used up, but does not authorize replacement of such parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: Aiken v. Manchester Flint Works (1865). Distinguishes consumption of parts from right to make replacements that would practice another patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheriff's or foreclosure sales and implied license (judicial sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser at a sheriff's sale or foreclosure may acquire an implied license to use a patented machine sold in execution or foreclosure, but rights can be contested depending on circumstances; doctrine recognizes that denying such use would be prejudicial to creditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative discussion (Wilder v. Kent, Chambers v. Smith): judicial sales of patented machines typically carry the beneficial rights of the defendant in execution; contrast with forced sales of intangible copyright plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of materials only does not permit making the patented article unless materials are exclusively for that use
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser of the materials of which an article consists, or of elements of which it is combined, obtains no right to make and use the article, unless the sold object can be used only in constructing the patented article — in which case sale implies license for that specific use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recapitulates §825: ensures that mere component sales don't authorize practicing the combination; exception protects obvious single-use components (Roosevelt v. Western Electric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee can sell with restrictions; such restrictions bind vendee
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may sell a patented article with restrictions as to its use, and these will bind the vendee if properly imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Holliday v. Matheson, DoTsey Revolving Harvester Rake Co. v. Bradley Mfg. Co. Sellers should specify restrictions clearly in deed/contract to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license does not authorize infringement of other patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an unconditional sale implies a license to use that article relative to the patent covering it, the sale does not import permission to use the article in a way that will violate the vendor's exclusive property in another invention (i.e., other patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: purchaser of machine covered by one patent may still infringe a separate process patent by using it (Downton v. Yaeger Milling Co.).
